title: Desi Arnaz
description: Cuban-American musician, actor, producer and television studio head (1917–1986)
wiki_lead:
Desiderio Alberto Arnaz y de Acha III (March 2, 1917 – December 2, 1986), known as Desi Arnaz, was a Cuban-American actor, musician, producer, and bandleader. Born in Santiago de Cuba, he fled with his family to Miami after the Cuban Revolution of 1933. He played Ricky Ricardo on the American television sitcom I Love Lucy, in which he co-starred with his wife Lucille Ball. Arnaz and Ball are credited as the innovators of the syndicated rerun, which they pioneered with the I Love Lucy series. 
Arnaz and Lucille Ball co-founded and ran the television production company Desilu Productions, originally to market I Love Lucy to television networks. After I Love Lucy ended, Arnaz went on to produce several other television series, at first with Desilu Productions, and later independently, including The Ann Sothern Show and The Untouchables. He was also the bandleader of his Latin group, the Desi Arnaz Orchestra. He was known for playing conga drums and popularized the conga line in the United States.

Desiderio Alberto Arnaz y de Acha III (March 2, 1917 – December 2, 1986), known as Desi Arnaz, was a Cuban-American actor, musician, producer, and bandleader. Born in Santiago de Cuba, he fled with his family to Miami after the Cuban Revolution of 1933. He played Ricky Ricardo on the American television sitcom I Love Lucy, in which he co-starred with his wife Lucille Ball. Arnaz and Ball are credited as the innovators of the syndicated rerun, which they pioneered with the I Love Lucy series. 
Arnaz and Lucille Ball co-founded and ran the television production company Desilu Productions, originally to market I Love Lucy to television networks. After I Love Lucy ended, Arnaz went on to produce several other television series, at first with Desilu Productions, and later independently, including The Ann Sothern Show and The Untouchables. He was also the bandleader of his Latin group, the Desi Arnaz Orchestra. He was known for playing conga drums and popularized the conga line in the United States.


Early life
Arnaz was born in Santiago de Cuba, Cuba, to Desiderio Alberto Arnaz y de Alberni II (March 8, 1894 – May 31, 1973) and Dolores "Lolita" de Acha y de Socias (April 2, 1896 – October 24, 1988). His father, a medical doctor trained in the United States, was Santiago's youngest mayor and also served in the Cuban House of Representatives. His maternal grandfather was Alberto de Acha, an executive at rum producer Bacardi & Co.
In his memoir, Arnaz states his ancestors Don Manuel and Ventura were given land grants in California, areas in Ventura County, Beverly Hills and the Wilshire district in Los Angeles by Queen Isabella II of Spain.
Arnaz was of Spanish, Irish and French descent.
A descendant of Cuban nobility, Arnaz was a great-great-great-grandson of José Joaquín, a mayor of Santiago de Cuba. The Cuban Revolution of 1933 forced Arnaz and his family to lose everything and flee Cuba. A mob attacked and destroyed the family's houses, property, and livestock. Arnaz narrowly escaped the attack because he was able to hop in a car driving away. His father, Alberto Arnaz, was jailed and all of his property was confiscated. He was released after six months when his father-in-law, Alberto de Acha, intervened on his behalf.
The family then fled to Miami, where Desi attended school. One of his classmates was Albert "Sonny" Capone, the only child of Chicago mobster Al Capone. Desi initially lived in Miami with only his father, with his mother coming to the United States at a later date and the parents divorcing in the time afterwards.  Arnaz's family came to the U.S. with no money and he had to live with his father in a garage that was infested with rats and roaches. In the summer of 1934, Arnaz attended Saint Leo Prep (near Tampa) to improve his English. His first jobs included working at Woolworth's and cleaning canary cages in Miami. He then went into the tile business with his father before turning to show business full time.

As a performer, Arnaz gained fame in the 1930s and 1940s as a conga drummer and bandleader, introducing Latin music rhythms like the conga line to American audiences through his orchestra's tours and recordings. His acting breakthrough came in the 1939 Broadway production Too Many Girls, where he met actress Lucille Ball; the pair married in 1940 and later co-starred as Ricky and Lucy Ricardo in the CBS sitcom I Love Lucy (1951â1957), which became a cultural phenomenon. Arnaz revolutionized television production by insisting on filming I Love Lucy on 35mm film using a multiple-camera setup before a live studio audience, rather than live broadcasts or inferior kinescope recordings, enabling high-quality reruns and pioneering syndication as a revenue model. Through Desilu Productions, co-founded with Ball in 1950, he oversaw the creation of iconic soundstages at former RKO Studios and produced enduring series such as The Untouchables, Star Trek, and The Andy Griffith Show, transforming Hollywood's approach to episodic television. Despite professional triumphs, Arnaz's personal life included struggles with alcoholism and infidelity, contributing to his 1960 divorce from Ball after two decades of marriage, though they maintained a collaborative relationship post-separation until he sold his Desilu stake in 1962. Arnaz retired from production in the late 1960s, made occasional acting appearances, and succumbed to lung cancer at age 69.
